{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-hi-x","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"32cf7469230107d05a8285e9ee0398cffc08ee49ccebbacaa25f56cbec0140c5","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-hi-class-3:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"1323c0f691f132d6e9e9a263c68306b972b82c8bbaa5a48a33a79177660764be","source_liveness_sha256":"27cf6d56fae2d5323c61bcbb69f0d992aeceb71a7dae4302b1f14baa17651cb0"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"The Driver: Judgment, Emotions, Medical Condition and Age","heading":"C — The Driver: Judgment, Emotions, Medical Condition and Age","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — The Driver: Judgment, Emotions, Medical Condition and Age

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Every driving situation involves three basic elements, the environment of highway and traffic, the vehicle, and the driver, and only the driver can gather information, apply skill, knowledge, experience and judgment, and take the action needed to complete the trip safely [A01].
Why it matters: the three-element model is the chapter's framing and a likely recall item.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Good judgment can help make up for lower levels of skill, knowledge or experience, but poor judgment can cancel out any degree of expertise, and your judgment is shaped mainly by your attitude when you drive [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
If you are worried, distracted or preoccupied you cannot count on being alert enough to drive safely, and troubles at home, quarrels, financial worries, serious family illness, personal fears or overconfidence can make you temporarily crash-prone [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
A person who has just had a violent argument, or who is angry or grieving, needs some cooling-off time before driving, because taking out frustration or anger on the road is very poor judgment and an expensive way to vent emotion [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Worry and safe driving do not mix, so if you are worried, ill, nervous, frightened, angry or depressed you should let someone else drive [A01].
Why it matters: the manual's rule is to hand over the keys, not to drive carefully while upset.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
A well-adjusted person is more likely to be a good driver, and you must act with consideration and courtesy toward other road users rather than only from your own point of view [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
Because full control of the vehicle rests with the driver, your attitude behind the wheel and how you use that power reveal whether you are a bully, a thoughtless lawbreaker or a self-centered lane stealer, or a reliable, courteous and emotionally mature person ready to share the road [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A01
Your physical condition has an important bearing on safe driving, and alcohol, drugs, illness or disability may cause or contribute to a traffic crash [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A01
Crash data show that the youngest drivers, those under age twenty, crash about twice as often as their share of all drivers would predict [A01].
Why it matters: the under-twenty group is the clearest statistic on the page.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A01
As driver age increases crashes keep falling until about age fifty to fifty-four, and drivers in that range have the fewest crashes of any age group [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A01
Beginning at age fifty-five crashes occur more often as age increases, and drivers over seventy-five have more crashes than middle-aged drivers but still fewer than drivers under twenty-five [A01].
Why it matters: the comparison to drivers under twenty-five is the trap: older drivers rise but do not pass the youngest group.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
Young adults want acceptance and recognition of their capabilities, and as drivers they sometimes demonstrate those capabilities beyond the limits of the vehicle, the road and even the most skillful drivers, which often ends in disaster [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
A young driver avoids that trap by resisting the desire to exhibit and compete, which only shows inexperience and immaturity, and by declining every challenge to prove personal or vehicle capability, which is adequate proof of maturity and responsibility [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
Driving experience usually increases skill and drivers become safer with the years up to a point, but aging eventually brings reduced hearing and eyesight, less physical dexterity and longer reaction time, longer decision time, and a shorter attention span [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
Older drivers very often fail to recognize the gradual decline in their ability to cope with driving situations and so become increasingly dangerous to themselves and others [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
Every driver, including the older experienced driver, should keep physically fit, have an annual physical examination, know how medications affect driving, recognize and drive within personal limitations, and seek and follow a physician's advice about driving capability [A02].
Why it matters: the five-point list is the chapter's prescription and a natural multi-part question.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0025]

Misconceptions: drivers over seventy-five do have more crashes than the middle-aged group, but they still have fewer than drivers under twenty-five, so the youngest group remains the highest; the safest age band is about fifty to fifty-four, not the newest drivers with the sharpest reflexes; the manual's cure for anger or worry is to let someone else drive, not to drive extra carefully.

Mnemonics: Twice the crashes under twenty, fewest at fifty to fifty-four, rising again from fifty-five, and over seventy-five still below under twenty-five; upset means let someone else drive.

Glossary: three elements of driving (environment, vehicle and driver); crash-prone (temporarily more likely to crash because of emotion or distraction); reaction time (the delay between seeing a hazard and acting); decision time (the delay in choosing what to do in a driving situation).

Dynamic facts: the age-band crash figures are statistical generalizations printed in this edition without a cited survey year and could change with newer data; the behavioral guidance is stable.
